My primary goal as an instructor is to make sure every student feels safe, welcome,
and respected, and knows they belong in the mathematics classroom. Students arrive
with very different experiences of mathematics, and some have had far more support
and encouragement than others. I share the conviction behind
[Federico Ardila-Mantilla's axioms for mathematics education](https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/201610/rnoti-p1164.pdf){.gold-link}
that mathematical talent is distributed equally across groups of people, and every student deserves meaningful
mathematical experiences and to be treated with dignity and respect.

Below are some aspects of my teaching philosophy, and how they show up in the courses
I have taught. My full [teaching statement (PDF)](../files/teaching-statement.pdf) has
more detail.

## Teaching philosophy {#philosophy}

### In the classroom

- **Doing mathematics, not just watching it.** After introducing a concept and working
  an example, I give students time to try a related problem before I present a
  solution. I walk around the room, offering small hints and asking questions that
  help them find a next step.
- **Mistakes are part of the work.** When a student is unsure or makes a mistake, my
  first concern is to help them feel at ease. An incomplete idea is still worth
  discussing, and I openly acknowledge my own mistakes.
- **Finding the right picture.** A good picture often makes sense before a formal
  statement does. In MTH 314 I used geometric transformations of the plane so that
  students understood what eigenvalues and eigenvectors tell us about a linear
  transformation while they learned to compute them.
- **Asking why, not just how.** My MTH 317H worksheets ask why a concept is useful or
  needed, not only how to apply it.

### Learning together

Explaining an idea to a classmate is one of the best ways to understand it, and
asking a classmate is often easier than asking the instructor. In person, I build
group work into class time. Online, where students rarely get to meet their peers, I
design the course so that live sessions are spent working on problems together.

### Caring for the whole student

- **Flexibility.** My students have lives and pressures outside my course. When a
  student faces difficult circumstances, I offer flexible deadlines so they can
  complete the work rather than fall behind for reasons beyond their control.
- **A fair chance to prepare.** I space exams so students have time to prepare, and I
  avoid scheduling one right after a long weekend or break.
- **Reaching out.** In an online course a struggling student can easily go unnoticed.
  I write to students who are not doing well and meet with them individually.
- **Another chance to show mastery.** With standards-based grading, an unsuccessful
  attempt becomes a reason to keep working rather than a final verdict.

### Feedback

I check understanding with short exit tickets and low-stakes worksheets, and I release
complete solutions after each deadline so students can check their own reasoning. I
also keep listening to what students tell me about their learning, and adjust.

### Technology, including AI

I use technology where it serves learning: live writing on an iPad projected to every
table, recorded videos, Zoom options for bad-weather days, and Python assignments for
the computational side of linear algebra. In MTH 317H recitations I give students
poorly written AI-generated proofs and ask them to find unjustified assumptions,
missing steps, and errors that are easy to overlook when an explanation sounds
convincing, and to say what the AI did well. The aim is for students to understand
both what AI can and cannot do, and to gain confidence in judging an argument for
themselves. AI should not do their homework.

## Teaching in different settings {#contexts}

**MTH 103A: College Algebra I** (instructor, Spring 2025). About sixty students in an
active-learning classroom in the MSU Union, with round tables and screens throughout
the room. Students worked in groups while two undergraduate learning assistants and I
moved between tables. The class met daily at 8 a.m. through a Michigan winter, so I
offered a Zoom option for icy mornings and possible closures. I wrote my own notes and
worksheets and used standards-based grading.

**MTH 124: Survey of Calculus** (instructor, Summer 2023, online). I ran the course as
a flipped classroom: students watched videos I recorded before class, so our live
sessions could be spent working through problems and discussing solutions together.
The course used Piazza for questions, and students could optionally record a short
video introducing themselves to help them find classmates to work with.

**MTH 314: Matrix Algebra with Applications** (instructor, Summer 2024, online). I wrote
lecture notes in LaTeX and also shared the handwritten notes from each Zoom lecture,
so students had both a polished reference and a record of how each argument unfolded.
I recorded lecture videos and short check-ins between meetings, and designed in-class
Python assignments.

**MTH 317H: Honors Linear Algebra** (recitation leader, Fall 2026). I teach the proof
techniques from MTH 299 that students need but may not yet know. The notes and
worksheets are on the [course page](mth317h-fs26.qmd).

## Student feedback {#student-feedback}

A few comments from end-of-semester student surveys:

> "One of the nicest professors I have interacted with at MSU." (MTH 314)

> "He treats all the students respectfully and replies to our queries quickly."

> "The teacher always provided examples with his explanations and double checked with
> the class to make sure we were understanding concepts." (MTH 314)

> "We learned what these concepts actually represented in linear algebra rather than
> just the routine calculations." (MTH 314)

> "Rather than simply showing the calculations for a problem, we actually went over
> what the concepts actually were." (MTH 314)

> "The course videos and notes helped provide a good way to study, and the ICs
> [in-class assignments] were an interesting way to practice math problems using
> code." (MTH 314)

> "The graded and ungraded work had similar scopes of difficulty so I felt it was good
> practice." (MTH 314)

> "Homework was appropriately balanced between difficulty and length." (MTH 818)

## Professional development {#cct}

I am completing MSU's
[Certification in College Teaching](https://grad.msu.edu/professional-development/graduate-educator-advancement-and-teaching/certification-in-college-teaching)
(expected Spring 2027), which includes the course MTHE 879, Teaching College
Mathematics, and the Certification in College Teaching Institute (May 2026). Workshops
I attended at the Institute:

- *Understanding the University Context: Aligning Teaching with Different
  Institutional Types and Missions*, Dr. Judith Stoddart (Vice Provost, University Arts
  and Collections)
- *Creating Effective Learning Environments*, Dr. Kirstin Parkin (Associate Professor,
  Microbiology and Molecular Genetics)
- *Assessing Student Learning*, Dr. Rique Campa (Professor and Senior Associate Dean,
  Graduate School)
- *Incorporating Technology in Teaching*, Dr. Stefanie Baier

Conversations with classmates from several disciplines have encouraged me to give
students more choice in how they show understanding. Where a course allows it, I would
like to offer projects such as a video, an artwork, or a physical model.

## Resources for students {#resources}

### Learning and reading

- [3Blue1Brown](https://www.youtube.com/@3blue1brown): visual explanations of
  mathematics, including a series on linear algebra
- [Keith Conrad's expository papers](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/): clear,
  self-contained notes on algebra and number theory
- [Terence Tao's career advice](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/career-advice/): essays on
  studying and working in mathematics
- [*Book of Proof*](https://richardhammack.github.io/BookOfProof/) by Richard Hammack,
  [*Linear Algebra Done Right*](https://linear.axler.net) by Sheldon Axler, and
  [*Linear Algebra Done Wrong*](https://www.math.brown.edu/streil/papers/LADW/LADW.html)
  by Sergei Treil, all free online
- [Springer textbooks](https://link.springer.com): many can be downloaded free through
  [MSU Libraries](https://lib.msu.edu); sign in with your MSU NetID
- [OpenStax](https://openstax.org): free, peer-reviewed college textbooks

### Tools

- [Desmos](https://www.desmos.com/calculator): online graphing calculator
- [Wolfram|Alpha](https://www.wolframalpha.com): computational answer engine
- [Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com): write mathematics in LaTeX in the browser

### At MSU

- [Mathematics Learning Center](https://math.msu.edu/mlc): free drop-in tutoring for
  MTH courses
- [MSU Food Bank](https://foodbank.msu.edu)
- [Counseling and Psychiatric Services (CAPS)](https://caps.msu.edu)
- [Resource Center for Persons with Disabilities (RCPD)](https://rcpd.msu.edu)

### Math and science programs in the Lansing area

- [MSU summer math camps](https://math.msu.edu/Outreach/2026-summer-math-camps/index.aspx),
  run by the MSU Department of Mathematics
- [Middle School Girls Math and Science Day](https://spartanyouth.msu.edu/resources/m/middle-school-girls-math-and-science-day),
  hosted at MSU by Graduate Women in Science
